title: Quantum Gates: X, Y, Z, H, and CNOT
summary: Learn what each supported gate does to a state, why phase gates can be invisible in one measurement basis, and why two Hadamards undo each other.
objectives: Describe the action of X, Y, Z, H, and CNOT.
Distinguish a bit flip from a phase change.
Explain why H followed by H is the identity.
Predict the control and target roles of a CNOT.

sections.heading: Gates are reversible transformations
body: A quantum gate transforms amplitudes while preserving normalization. Every gate in this MVP is reversible: applying the same gate twice restores the original state for X, Y, Z, H, and CNOT.
Gate order matters. The circuit is an ordered list of instructions, not a set of symbols on a diagram.

sections.heading: X, Y, and Z
body: X is the quantum NOT gate. It swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩, so X|0⟩ = |1⟩. In the computational basis it is a bit flip.
Y also flips the bit, but it adds a phase factor. Z leaves |0⟩ and |1⟩ unchanged except for a minus sign on |1⟩: Z|0⟩ = |0⟩ and Z|1⟩ = −|1⟩.
A phase is not visible if you immediately measure in the computational basis. It becomes visible when later gates make the paths interfere.

sections.heading: H changes the measurement basis
body: H maps |0⟩ to |+⟩ and |1⟩ to |−⟩. It creates equal-magnitude superpositions, and it also converts phase information into bit information.
Because H is its own inverse, two H gates in a row are the identity. The example circuit demonstrates this with a deterministic 0 outcome.

sections.heading: CNOT is a two-qubit gate
body: CNOT (written cx) flips its target qubit exactly when its control qubit is |1⟩. If the control is |0⟩, nothing happens to the target.
On a computational-basis input, CNOT is reversible and its action is its own inverse. It is also the standard tool for creating entanglement when the control is in a superposition.
In the builder, CNOT is one step spanning two wires. Choose a control and a different target; the diagram draws a control dot and a target circle.

sections.heading: Try the reversible example
body: The sample circuit applies H twice to q0 and then measures. The ideal outcome is always 0.
Try replacing the two H gates with one H, run, and observe the 50/50 sampling. Then add a Z between the two H gates to see how phase changes the final interference.

expected_behavior: Two consecutive H gates return q0 to |0⟩, so every shot measures 0.
A single H produces both 0 and 1 in roughly equal proportions.
Z alone on |0⟩ still measures 0 because it changes phase, not the computational-basis outcome.

check_questions.question: Which gate flips |0⟩ to |1⟩?
check_questions.explanation: X is the bit-flip gate. Z adds a phase, H creates a superposition, and CNOT needs a control qubit.

check_questions.question: Why does Z followed by measurement give 0 for a qubit initially in |0⟩?
options: Z maps |0⟩ to |0⟩, and the phase on |1⟩ is not observed in this basis
Z always forces a measurement result of 0 on every state
check_questions.explanation: Z|0⟩ = |0⟩. Even for |1⟩, Z only adds a minus sign, which a single computational-basis measurement cannot distinguish.

check_questions.question: In CNOT q0→q1, when does q1 flip?
check_questions.explanation: The first qubit is the control. The target flips only when the control is in |1⟩.
